You're treating everything as though it's an inevitable result of economics, which it really isn't. 

After WW2 there was a huge shortage of houses in UK, so they made the political choice to build millions and the political choice to introduce huge rent caps. Since then the dominant voting block (older people) have decided to turn their cheap necessities into an investment so the UK is making different political decision which is why housing is extortionate here. 'Amount of land in areas with good jobs' implies an absolute limit that can never be increased but in fact up until the 90s it was fairly routine for goverments to respond to these problems with huge investments to make new areas with good jobs.

You say rent has stayed flat at 35% of income in the UK, but the sizes of the rental properties are halving or quartering so it's actually a 2-4X increase in price relative to wages. 

And the argument that concerts and childcare have tripled in price in terms of numbers of hours worked, because those people still need to earn a living would imply that people working in daycares and people working as classical musicians went from being one of the least well paid gigs to one of the most well paid one. If it was just a normal inflationary rise then the cost would remain flat in terms of number of hours worked. 

It's only about the price of land. Childcare costs go mostly towards rent and profit (not the people working in the buildings). Concert costs go mostly towards rent and building maintenance (not the classical musicians), And infrastructure keeps costing more and more because the NIMBYism and deliberate property price inflation by a landowning generation means that even when we do construction, it's more expensive because there are fewer opportunities, so less competition, so fewer skilled workers in that area, and fewer economies of scale. Housing in the US manages to stay cheap by hugely reducing build quality to an extent that is illegal in the other countries and exploiting undocumented workers, but again that's missing the huge maintenance costs involved since new builds will start to break pretty soon in the US. 

Idk if the intention was to try and be reassuring, but the reality is luxuries have become cheaper and cheaper while the absolute necessities normalised for size and actual hours worked (not just percentage of a couple's salary have skyrocketed (rent and groceries). Now groceries is in large part also global warming (which also deserves a mention) but rent is entirely about a political choice made in every country to build cheap housing for boomers so they'd have an easy start, and then let them take away that safety net and turn housing into an investment so they'd have a cushy retirement off the backs of the younger generations. 



A country where rent and groceries are cheap but you have to work your arse off for nice holidays and a TV is a great country to live in with excellent incentives and indicates prosperity.

A country where nice holidays and TV and smartphones are cheap but you have to work your arse off to eat and have shelter is a corrupt shithole. That's the difference, that's why everyone's disturbed at the route every country is going down. It has never been easier to have it all.
